messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Meena was twenty-four when she was taken. She had been working late at her family’s tailoring shop in a small city in northern India, finishing a wedding lengha for a client whose measurements she’d taken that morning. Three men came through the back door. They accused her of harboring documents for a student activist group her brother had briefly been involved with. For six hours, they kept her in a windowless room behind the shop, beating her with a rubber hose and a wooden plank, and at intervals forcing her to kneel on a steel grille while they pressed lit cigarettes into her forearms and the backs of her hands. She was certain she would die there, that no one would find her, that her mother would simply receive a body. She did not give them any names because she did not have any, but they did not believe her. When they finally left, she crawled to the front of the shop and called her brother, who took her to a hospital. The police did nothing. Her parents moved her to the United States within the month, to live with an aunt in New Jersey, and Meena never spoke of the night again.

Now she is twenty-eight, married to a man she met through her aunt, and working as a tailor in a dry-cleaning shop in a strip mall outside Newark. She is good at her job—quick, precise, reliable—but she has not been to a doctor since she arrived in the country. When her husband suggested she get a physical, she told him she did not have time. When her arm began to ache from the old scar tissue, she wrapped it in a cloth and kept sewing. She does not seek medical or psychological help because the thought of sitting in a waiting room, of being asked to undress or answer questions, makes her feel as though the walls are shrinking. What frightens her most is not the pain itself but the vulnerability—the exposure of her body to a stranger’s gaze, the possibility of being trapped in a small room with a closed door. She has come to believe that medical settings are places where people are hurt, not helped, and that the safest thing is to stay away.

She scans for exits as soon as she enters any room or building. At the dry-cleaning shop, she has positioned her sewing table so that she faces the front door directly, with a clear line of sight to the back alley exit behind the pressing machine. She cannot work any other way. When customers walk in and block her view of the door, she feels a rush of heat in her chest and has to force herself to breathe. She is hypervigilant in a way that exhausts her—she notices every footstep behind her, every shadow that passes the front window, every car that slows down near the shop. She cannot relax. Even at home, in the evenings, she finds herself unable to sit still. Her husband will put on a movie, and she will watch the door instead of the screen. She has tried to let herself rest, but the moment she does, her mind floods with images of the grille, the hose, the smell of her own burning skin. She avoids relaxing because it feels dangerous, as though letting her guard down will invite the men back into her life.

The connection between her constant sense of threat and her strategies for managing it has become a tight loop she cannot step out of. Every time she scans for an exit, she reminds herself that danger is possible. Every time she avoids a doctor’s appointment, she confirms that the world is unsafe. She has stopped going to the grocery store alone, stopped visiting her aunt in the city, stopped accepting evening alterations that would require her to stay late at the shop. Her husband has begun to worry. He asked her, gently, if she might talk to someone. She said no. But last week, a customer came in with a wedding sari for hemming, and Meena’s hands began to shake so violently that she had to excuse herself to the back room. She stood there, staring at the fire exit, and realized that she could not keep living this way—always watching, always bracing, always alone with the room in her head. She is afraid that if she opens the door to her fear, it will never close. But she is also afraid that if she does not, she will lose everything she has built.
